Article Title: What's cooking? A kitchen fix to cut dementia risk in old age
Article Text:
Cooking is a complex task from neurological point of view: Doc

New Delhi: What if one of the simplest ways to keep the brain active later in life is already sitting in the kitchen? A six-year study from Japan has found that older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care than those who cooked less often.The population-based study followed 10,978 adults aged 65 years and older and recorded 1,195 cases of dementia during the six-year follow-up. After accounting for demographic, socioeconomic and health-related factors, men who cooked at least once a week had a 23% lower risk of dementia, while women had a 27% lower risk, compared with those who cooked less than once a week. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. Among them, more frequent home cooking was associated with a 67% lower risk of dementia in older adults.The findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, were based on data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study. Researchers assessed cooking frequency and skills at the beginning of the study and then tracked dementia requiring care through Japan's public long-term care insurance records.Dr (Col) Joy Dev Mukherji, chairman and head, neurology, Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, said cooking is a surprisingly complex activity from a neurological point of view. "It involves planning, attention, working memory, while also combining movement and sensory stimulation," he said. However, he cautioned against interpreting the findings as proof that cooking prevents dementia.“This was an observational study and does not prove that cooking prevents dementia. It is also possible that people in the early stages of cognitive decline may gradually stop cooking because of difficulties with planning and memory,” he said.Dr Manjari Tripathi, head of neurology at AIIMS, highlighted the social dimension of cooking, saying preparing meals with friends, family or the wider community could provide additional cognitive and social engagement. She also encouraged men to cook, saying the activity must not be viewed as restricted to women.Interestingly, the association was strongest among people with lower cooking skills, possibly because less experienced cooks engage more in planning and problem-solving. However, this was not established by the study. Doctors said the broader message is to remain engaged in meaningful activities involving learning, planning, movement and social interaction, rather than viewing cooking as a treatment for dementia.
Article Summary: Six-year study from japan found older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. Doctors said the broader message is to remain engaged in meaningful activities involving learning, planning, movement and social interaction.

Article Title: In a first, 9 Isro staff bodies seek 'written clarity' on private sector shift
Article Text:
The joint representation has been signed by the Isro Staff Association, SAC Employees Welfare Association and others.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: For the first time since the government began opening India’s space sector to private industry six years ago, nine employee bodies at Isro centres representing thousands of staff under the Department of Space (DoS), have formally raised concerns over the direction and basis of the transition. They have sought written clarification from chairman, space commission, who also serves as secretary, DoS and chairman, Isro.“Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned Isro. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces Isro to a residual R&D boutique while the realisation of the nation’s launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands,” the representation dated Sept 4 and accessed by TOI, reads.Terming technology developed by Isro a national asset, they said its transfer must be transparent, accountable, and consistent with strategic, safety and employment considerations. “...Serving employees have an earned right to be informed, consulted and protected. Natural justice and good administration require that policy of this magnitude be explained to the workforce by the Department itself.”The joint representation has been signed by the Isro Staff Association, SHAR Employees Association, Isac Employees Association, Isro Staff Association-LPSC, Isro Staff Association-BBU, NRSA Employees Union, Space Employees Association-BBU, Isro Staff Association-IPRC and SAC Employees Welfare Association.Pointing to a recent public statement reportedly made by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka on Isro eventually “not manufacturing any launch vehicles”, they asked if his statement “represents an approved decision of the Govt of India, Space Commission or DoS… If approved, the date, authority and text of the policy decision may kindly be indicated.”“What will be the future mandated role of Isro — specifically, whether design, development, realisation, integration, testing and launch of PSLV, LVM-3, SSLV and successor vehicles will continue as Isro functions or will cease. Whether any decision has been taken to exclude PSUs from the proposed transfer of PSLV/LVM-3 production, and the justification for such exclusion,” they asked.They also sought in writing the institutional arrangement under which publicly created technology, test facilities, launch complexes and know-how — built with taxpayer funds and the labour of generations of Isro employees — are being transferred or opened to private operation, and the role of NSIL vis-a-vis IN-SPACe in such transfers.“Isro was built as a national scientific institution with public funds, public purpose and a public workforce. Launch-vehicle design, realisation, integration, testing and launch operations are not merely ‘manufacturing contracts’. They are the core competence, institutional memory and strategic capability of the organisation,” the representation reads.They said they have reasonable fear that a progressive withdrawal of Isro from launch-vehicle and satellite realisation will tamper experiments after research, shrink in-house work, freeze or reduce sanctioned strength, and close promotion and skill-development avenues in technical, scientific, administrative, stores, purchase, quality, safety and industrial cadres.“Existing employees may be rendered surplus, or redeployed, or left without meaningful work while the same tasks are performed by private contractors using publicly developed technology…Regular recruitment to Group A, B and C posts — already constrained by vacancies and attrition — will further decline, denying opportunity to meritorious youth who look to Isro as a public career of honour, not as a private contractor's workforce,” the letter reads.Congratulating Isro on the success of the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission, the letter read: “...We once again proved that we can rise from ashes and fly like a phoenix.”“We submit this in a constructive and democratic spirit. Our loyalty to Isro and to the national space programme isn’t in question. Precisely because of that loyalty, we consider it our duty to seek clarity before uncertainty hardens into irreversible policy,” they said, adding that they will plan further course of action once the written reply is received.
Article Summary: Nine employee bodies at isro centres have formally raised concerns over the direction and basis of the transition. They have sought written clarification from chairman, space commission, who also serves as secretary, dos and chairman, isro. The joint representation has been signed by the isro staff association, sac employees welfare association and others.

Article Title: Work-life balance vs job security: The workplace trade-off Gen Z is challenging
Article Text:
The salary still matters

Security feels increasingly fragile

How much sacrifice is acceptable?

The stereotype problem

What does the survey indicate?

Young workers are entering a labour market shaped by layoffs, artificial intelligence, intense competition and constantly changing skill requirements. At the same time, they have grown increasingly vocal about boundaries, mental health and the value of time outside the office.As the generational composition of the workforce continues to evolve, organisations seem to face new challenges in designing effective employee engagement strategies. Shaped by rapid technological change and globalisation, millennials and Generation Z bring distinct work values, communication preferences and expectations around career growth, flexibility and the workplace.For Gen Z, the ideal job increasingly sounds like a carefully negotiated deal: pay me well, give me room to grow, let me have a life after work and, preferably, give me some control over how I get the work done.A survey of young workers reflects that tension. Job security emerged as an important consideration, but work-life balance carried an equally strong pull. The responses suggest a generation trying to answer a difficult question: how much career stability is worth sacrificing personal freedom for?The survey found that 95% of respondents rated job security at the higher end of the importance scale, with 57.1% giving it the highest rating.At the same time, 90.5% also gave work-life balance equal weight.That makes the dilemma rather clear. Gen Z wants security. It also wants breathing room.The idea of Gen Z choosing lifestyle over money tells only one part of the story. The responses from young workers point to a more complicated calculation.Financial independence and building a successful career were each selected by 76.2% of respondents as among their biggest reasons for working. Achieving a particular lifestyle followed at 61.9%, while gaining experience and skills came in at 57.1%.Money remains a major part of the equation. Neeshu Shukla, a working professional from Delhi, said, “Better pay is important. Money is the deal breaker,” followed by timely hikes and promotions.For Shukla, however, the workplace equation extends beyond the payslip. She wants a professional but empathetic environment and opportunities to learn and grow. She also places value on skills, experience, capabilities and willingness to learn as the basis for determining an employee’s value.The broader survey reflects a similar hierarchy. Personal growth was the most-selected career priority apart from money, at 85.7%. Work-life balance followed at 66.7%, while good workplace culture stood at 61.9%. Career progression and job security were selected by 47.6% and 42.9%, respectively.The anxiety around stability also has a very practical source. Competition and low salaries were the biggest source of career insecurity in the survey, selected by 76.2% of respondents. Layoffs followed at 52.4%, while lack of job opportunities and lack of career growth each stood at 47.6%. Economic uncertainty was another concern for 42.9% of respondents. AI and automation were cited by 38.1%.That anxiety shows up in how respondents view the very idea of a “secure job”. More than seven in 10 said such security exists only in certain industries. Just 19% considered a secure job realistic in the broader economy.A recent Emeritus report titled ‘India’s Gen Z Outlook 2026’ found a similar shift in how young Indians think about careers. The study found that 74% of Gen Z respondents prioritise work-life balance over formal leadership titles, while 65% believe a successful career does not require becoming an executive leader.That finding adds another layer to the workplace debate. The traditional image of career success often comes with a predictable sequence: climb the ladder, take on more responsibility, earn more money and eventually reach a senior title.Gen Z appears to be questioning how attractive that ladder remains.Ashwin Damera, co-founder and CEO of Emeritus, described the shift as an overhaul of the traditional career path, driven by rapidly changing skills and jobs.The survey becomes particularly interesting when the questions move from preferences to trade-offs.Asked whether they would stay in a job they disliked if it offered excellent job security and financial stability, 19% said probably yes. Another 33.3% remained unsure, while 42.9% said probably not.Over 42% of respondents said they would immediately leave a high-paying job that seriously affected their mental health or personal life. A further 19% said their decision would depend on their financial situation.For Kajal Singh, an HR professional working at a consultancy firm in Delhi, the workplace she wants comes down to “flexible work options, better work-life balance & a supportive environment.”Harshita, a working professional from Bhopal, takes the idea of flexibility further. In her ideal workplace, she wants “flexibility and respect for the opinions of Gen Zs,” along with room for employees to decide how they execute their work.The pattern is not confined to India. A separate Deloitte 2026 survey of Gen Zs and millennials found that 55% of Gen Zs and 52% of millennials are delaying major life decisions because of financial pressures. Only 25% of Gen Zs and 21% of millennials prefer rapid career progression through frequent promotions, while just 6% in both groups identify leadership as their primary career goal.At the same time, 74% of both Gen Zs and millennials use AI to some extent in their day-to-day work, with many viewing it as an opportunity to improve productivity and open new career paths — even as they feel they are adapting faster than their organisations.Taken together, the findings point to a generation caught between two competing demands: the need for financial security and the refusal to define success solely by the traditional career ladder.The generation also appears to be tired of having that negotiation interpreted as a lack of ambition.More than half of respondents said older generations completely misunderstand Gen Z’s attitude towards work, while another 42.9% said they misunderstand it somewhat.The most irritating stereotype was the idea that “Gen Z doesn't want to work”, selected by 81% of respondents. “Gen Z quits too easily” followed at 76.2%. Other commonly selected stereotypes included being lazy, expecting too much and having no loyalty.For employers, that makes the Gen Z workplace conversation less about choosing between stability and balance and more about whether the two can exist together. For young workers, the bigger challenge is figuring out which compromises build a career and which ones slowly consume the life that career was supposed to support.
Article Summary: A survey of young workers reflects that tension. Job security emerged as an important consideration, but work-life balance carried an equally strong pull. The responses suggest a generation trying to answer a difficult question: how much career stability is worth sacrificing personal freedom for?

India is moving away from a focus on only disaster response and relief towards disaster mitigation and resilience, said Sudarshan Suchi, chief development officer at Reliance Foundation, at a timely discussion on ‘Rebooting Development for Disaster Resilience’.The shift away from the emergency response approach includes preventing or reducing the worst impacts of disasters through better risk-informed planning, as well as enhancing the capacity of communities to cope with and recover from natural hazards, Suchi said. Reliance Foundation has a large disaster management programme working across several states. Increasingly, “all of our initiatives will be community-led,” Suchi said.Technology is aiding that shift, said Samhita R, co-founder and CEO of Resilience360, a start-up that offers AI-powered climate risk management solutions. Using large language models, its software can provide quick, hyperlocal risk assessments. That, she said, can help people make risk-informed decisions and “future-proof communities.”

Article Title: TOI Social Impact Summit: Frame business models for society, says ITC CMD Sanjiv Puri
Article Text:

ITC chairman and managing director Sanjiv Puri has said sustainability and inclusive growth must be an integral part of the corporate sector's business model, a model his conglomerate has followed."Economic progress cannot be seen in isolation from sustainability. Both have to go together... Corporates must create economic value, because that creates the foundation to go beyond. But it must be both economic and societal value. And that is what we call responsible competitiveness," Puri said in his keynote address at the TOI Social Impact Summit.He called upon organisations to go beyond creating shareholder value. "This is going to become increasingly important in the future, not merely because regulations are more and more evolving in this space, but such behaviour is being asked by regulators -whether the regulations are related to the environment or social systems. Global trade regulations are also emerging, but also stakeholders are demanding it. " He said it made business sense to work out models that help society.Puri said the world was facing multiple challenges from geopolitical turmoil to weaponisation of tariffs and the climate crisis, which were putting pressure on livelihood, and food and nutrition security."We are actually in a perfect storm. This convergence of challenges, uncertainty and rapid change call for novel strategies," he said, adding the vulnerable face maximum threat.He called for a joint effort from govt, the corporate sector and civil society to deal with climate change, while noting India has chosen a low carbon growth path.Citing ITC's example, he said it created an entire ecosystem- from R&D to growing trees that do not suck out water and working with small farmers-to reduce dependence on pulp for the paperboard business, a model extended to fruit juices.On CSR, Puri said it should be looked at as a business venture and its outcome evaluated. "You have to first invest in building capacity at the community level so that the initiatives are sustained and built upon. Otherwise, over a period of time, it can wither away."

Article Title: Output overdrive: 30% productivity boost could power 35% of future manufacturing
Article Text:
30% productivity boost could power 35% of future manufacturing

Small factories lag larger firms

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Six ways to drive manufacturing growth

Productivity

Workforce shifts

Global integration

Investment in capacity

Innovation and technology

Consumption-led growth.

India's manufacturing sector could get nearly 35 per cent of its future output simply by getting its workforce 30 per cent more productive.The finding comes from KPMG's analysis of more than 130 large Indian manufacturing companies over 10 years. It found that companies which improved productivity faster than their peers also saw stronger growth in profits and market value.Their net profits grew by around 10-11 per cent annually, compared with about 7 per cent for companies with average productivity.The difference was even wider in market value. Companies leading in productivity recorded around 19 per cent CAGR in market capitalisation, against nearly 10 per cent for average-productivity organisations.Overall, productivity-leading companies saw more than 50 per cent higher profitability growth and twice the market-cap expansion compared with their peers.The gains, however, are not spread evenly across the manufacturing sector.More than 70 per cent of large manufacturing companies would need transformative measures to achieve the productivity growth rate required for India's manufacturing ambition, the report said.There is also a wide gap between smaller and larger factories. Small and unorganised manufacturing facilities produce less than 20 per cent of the output per worker compared with large firms.Even among companies within the manufacturing sector, productivity can vary sharply, with differences ranging between 300 per cent and 1,000 per cent.KPMG identified six broad levers for manufacturing growth:But productivity stands out because its benefits can continue over time.“Productivity is Indian manufacturing's most powerful growth lever,” the report said, adding that productivity gains “embed permanently into the system, raising output, margins, and competitiveness year after year.”“Unlike scale or demand-led levers, productivity improvements embed permanently into the system,” the report said.The report said improving productivity would require companies to rethink how work is organised, how organisations are structured and how their workforce is deployed.Digital and AI tools, performance management and changes in workplace culture would also be needed to support these changes, it said.
Article Summary: 30% productivity boost could power 35% of future manufacturing output. Companies which improved productivity faster than their peers also saw stronger growth in profits and market value. Small and unorganised manufacturing facilities produce less than 20% of the output per worker compared with large firms.

Article Title: Silver prices crash over 40% from Rs 4 lakh/kg high to Rs 2.35 lakh, but buyers are still staying away; bigger problem yet to arrive as 2,000 tonnes ordered by Indian dealers risk piling up
Article Text:
Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins.

Silver Demand Weakens

Massive stockpiling of silver

Silver’s Spectacular Fall

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

A huge crash in silver prices should have led to a revival in demand, but investors seem to be staying away. And this has raised a fresh worry ahead of the festive season.Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. The situation comes even as silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.In Mumbai’s spot market, silver was trading at Rs 2.35 lakh per kg earlier this week.Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses, making them hesitant to make fresh purchases despite the steep correction in prices!Also Read | A couple sold gold for Rs 20 lakh to buy a home, another family got Rs 80 lakh for a US degree and business: How Indians are unlocking value of idle gold sitting in their lockers "Investment demand for silver ETFs, bars and coins has come down. Internationally, prices are unlikely to cross $100 per troy ounce immediately unless the US-Iran war comes to an end. Silver prices are undervalued," Chirag Sheth, global business head, Public Gold Bullion (SG) Pte told ET. "The continuous war between US and Iran has impacted the solar industry, semiconductor industry and EV industry where silver is used. "The weak demand is also creating an inventory problem for domestic players.Indian bullion dealers and refiners have reportedly placed orders for around 2,000 tonnes of silver, which is currently in transit. The additional supplies have raised concerns over a further build-up in stocks. India imports around 7,000 tonnes of silver every year."With no new investors coming in and no immediate signs of prices going up, refiners and bullion dealers are facing a problem internationally as well as in domestic markets," said James Jose, president, Precious Metals Refiners Forum.Silver prices have fallen steadily over the past seven months, following an extraordinary rally that pushed the metal more than 300% higher year-on-year. In January, silver crossed Rs 4 lakh per kg on the Multi Commodity Exchange for the first time."The market is still digesting the aftermath of the speculation-driven frenzy, and this may be prompting investors to stay away after many of them incurred significant losses," said Carsten Menke, head, Next Generation Research, Julius Baer told ET.The outlook for industrial demand is adding to the pressure, with consumption expected to weaken. "A shift to cheaper alternatives, such as aluminium and copper, has started, and the growth outlook for Chinese solar module makers, which are the biggest industrial users of silver, is not as strong anymore," Menke said.The ongoing US-Iran war has added to the negative sentiment surrounding silver. If the conflict continues for an extended period, investors may remain cautious. At the same time, expectations of weaker industrial consumption could make a rapid rebound in silver prices difficult.Despite the sharp fall, some long-term investors are once again looking at silver as a way to diversify their portfolios."The market has taken full cognisance of the marked decline in silver prices in recent days. Some investors have shaved off their allocation, while others have prepared for fresh acquisition depending on their views and goals," said Nilanjan Dey, partner, Wishlist Capital.Dey said investors who have a time horizon of five years or longer may look at buying silver ETFs in a staggered manner instead of putting in a large amount at one go. Monthly or fortnightly investments could help spread out the purchase price and reduce the impact of short-term price movements.For first-time investors looking to add precious metals to their portfolios as a diversification from equities, ETFs can provide exposure without the need to hold or manage physical silver. However, Dey warned that investors with a shorter investment horizon should not assume that the recent decline automatically makes silver an attractive buying opportunity.
Article Summary: Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the us-iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.

Article Title: Isro’s GSLV-F17 successfully places EOS-05 Earth observation satellite in geosynchronous orbit
Article Text:
ISRO’s GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission successfully accomplished

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SRIHARIKOTA: The Indian Space Research Organisation ( Isro ) successfully launched EOS-05, India’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit, aboard GSLV-F17 in the early hours of Friday.The 51.7-metre-tall, 420.5-tonne, three-stage rocket lifted off from the second launch pad at Sriharikota at 2.55am and placed the around 2,367kg Earth observation satellite in its intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit.This was the 19th GSLV flight. GSLV-F17 had a S139 solid core with four L40H liquid strap-ons, a GL40HT liquid second stage and a CUS15 indigenous cryogenic upper stage, besides a four-metre composite ogive payload fairing.EOS-05 was injected into a geosynchronous transfer orbit with a nominal perigee of 171km, apogee of 31026km and inclination of 19.28 degrees. The satellite will be moved to the final orbit through a series of manoeuvres using onboard thrusters.Isro chairman V Narayanan said the rocket injected the satellite in the intended orbit precisely. This is the 107th launch from Sriharikota and 19th GSLV flight. The chairman addressed from the mission control complex post launch."From launching 1536kg payload in the first GSLV launch, the chairman said the rocket has carried the heaviest payload in its history at 2367kg. We gradually improved the performance of the vehicle by optimising the structural mass and improving propulsion system. The satellite is India's first dedicating imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit. It will provide strategic data."The chairman also said Isro will have six more launches this financial year including navigation satellite NVS-03 and Gaganyaan first uncrewed mission.India had 21 operational Earth observation satellites as of February 2026. Of these, most are in low-Earth or sun-synchronous polar orbits, while India’s geostationary-orbit Earth observation capability is currently represented by the meteorological satellites INSAT-3D, INSAT-3DR and INSAT-3DS. EOS-05 is India’s first imaging satellite to operate from geosynchronous orbit.The launch was the first GSLV mission since GSLV-F16 successfully placed the joint Nasa-Isro NISAR Earth observation satellite in a 743km sun-synchronous orbit on July 30, 2025. Friday’s launch was Isro’s second orbital mission of 2026. The first, PSLV-C62 carrying EOS-N1 and other payloads on Jan 12, failed following an anomaly towards the end of the rocket’s third-stage flight.
Article Summary: Isro’s gslv-f17/eos-05 mission successfully accomplished on friday. The 51.7-metre-tall, 420.5-tonne, three-stage rocket lifted off from the second launch pad at sriharikota at 2.55am. The satellite is india's first dedicating imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit.

Article Title: Sophie Cunningham’s hilarious business idea with Diana Taurasi has fans imagining a WNBA yacht party
Article Text:
Sophie Cunningham. Image via: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Sophie Cunningham’s dream business has a Diana Taurasi twist

Sophie Cunningham’s growing profile beyond basketball

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sophie Cunningham has found plenty of ways to keep WNBA fans talking, both on and off the court. The Indiana Fever guard recently shared an unexpectedly ambitious idea for her dream business, and it has little to do with basketball. Her plan involves a yacht, endless sunshine, drinks and one of the biggest names in WNBA history, Diana Taurasi.Cunningham was asked what kind of business she would create if she could team up with another WNBA player. Instead of naming a teammate or choosing something connected to basketball, she went in a much more relaxed direction.Her pick was Taurasi, the legendary former WNBA star who built one of the most decorated careers in women's basketball. Cunningham's reason for choosing her potential business partner was refreshingly direct."If you were going to start a business with another WNBA player, who would it be?""I like that," she says in response to the question.After taking a moment to consider the idea, Cunningham revealed that she would choose Taurasi and build the business around a yacht."Because she has the finances," Cunningham explains.The concept sounds less like a traditional startup and more like a floating vacation for basketball fans.Cunningham imagined spending time on a boat, either on a lake or out at sea, with good weather, drinks and plenty of opportunities to relax."And then, the business would be being on a yacht, on a boat, on a lake or on the ocean, drinks flowing, you're getting a nice tan. But, definitely, budget, not mine."The comment captures Cunningham's playful personality. Rather than pitching a serious investment plan, she leaned into the fun of imagining what life could look like if money and logistics were not a concern.The interviewer then compared the concept to the reality series "Below Deck," which follows crews working aboard luxury yachts."You guys can start your own 'Below Deck?'""I like that," she says, laughing. "Absolutely."While a WNBA yacht venture with Taurasi remains a fantasy for now, Cunningham's growing popularity has opened plenty of doors away from basketball.The Fever guard recently passed 4 million followers on Instagram, giving her an enormous platform beyond the court. Article Title: ‘Floor-collected, broken noodles used to make bhujia': What FSSAI found at Wai-Wai's Rajasthan unit
Article Text:
India's food regulator FSSAI has ordered CG Foods India to stop producing veg bhujia





NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) has directed CG Foods India Pvt Ltd to stop production of its ‘Veg Bhujia Namkeen’ after an inspection at the company’s facility in Rajasthan found multiple food safety and hygiene violations.The food regulator said on Thursday that enforcement action had been initiated against the company over “unsafe processing, unlicensed bhujia manufacturing, and predated packaging”.During an inspection at the company’s unit in Roopangarh, Ajmer, officials found floor-collected and broken noodles being reprocessed into bhujia without heat treatment, FSSAI said.The inspection also uncovered the use of predated packaging and the unlicensed manufacture of ‘Wai-Wai MaMa’ and ‘Wai-Wai Mama Punte’ bhujia variants, allegedly in violation of Section 31(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said officials seized 32,107.2 kg of stock, including loose broken noodles, from the premises.The inspection further revealed deficiencies in hygiene and documentation, including inadequate pest-control records and other food safety lapses.Officials collected samples for laboratory testing and detained 1,925 boxes of expired finished products. Legal proceedings have also been initiated against the company.FSSAI directed CG Foods India to discontinue production of Veg Bhujia Namkeen products without the required approvals and corrective measures.The regulator said further action would be taken based on the laboratory test results and findings of the inspection.
Article Summary: India's food regulator fssai has ordered cg foods india to stop producing veg bhujia. During an inspection at the company’s unit in roopangarh, ajmer, officials found floor-collected and broken noodles. Legal proceedings have also been initiated against the company.

Article Title: Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang can't stop making fun of Google, says who is ...
Article Text:
Meta AI head

The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at Google

Where the gains came from

The cost advantage

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.Wang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).According to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.Beyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.

Article Title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai sends a message to his college IIT Kharagpur as it celebrates 75 years; shares happy memories as student: Meals at Harry's, studying in…
Article Text:
Image credit: Instagram

Sundar Pichai's IIT Kharagpur memories: Harry's, Illu and room B-308

Pichai's AI prediction: from labs to farmers, doctors and government offices

IIT Kharagpur at 75: why Pichai is betting on students

Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai has recorded a video message for IIT Kharagpur as the institute turns 75, and he spends most of it on the small stuff. Meals at Harry's. The Illu festival. Nights spent studying in room B-308. The wingmates, and the professors who stuck with him. Campus, he said, is also where he met his wife Anjali, where he first learned to program, and where he carried floppy disks around to get time on one of the few machines available. "These moments shaped the course of my life," he said, "putting me on a path to Google."That last line is the pivot. The message, posted by IIT Kharagpur on X, works as two things at once—a nostalgia reel and a forecast. Pichai, who graduated in 1993 with a B.Tech in metallurgical engineering, uses the anniversary to set out where he thinks artificial intelligence lands over the next five years, and to make a case that universities, not just tech companies, will decide whether any of it reaches people who aren't already using it.The specificity is what makes it land. B-308 in Nehru Hall is an unremarkable hostel room—bed, study table, chair, almirah—and it has quietly become a campus landmark, currently occupied by a final-year chemical engineering student.Metallurgy, meanwhile, sits nowhere near the top of India's engineering pecking order, which is part of why the room has the pull it does.Pichai called an education from the institute "truly a gift" and said IIT Kharagpur "played a formative role in shaping the lens through which I strive to make an impact on the world." He also noted how far its graduates have travelled, in India and outside it.The forward-looking half is the newsier one. "When I look at the next five years, I see AI moving away from the lab and the early adopters and into the hands of people doing the work," Pichai said—"the healthcare workers, the government officials, the farmers, developers, and entrepreneurs."The framing is deliberate. He is not describing AI as something to experiment with, but as something that sits inside jobs people already do. "We are building AI so that it can help all of us do our work at the next level and do it in a more fulfilling way," he added.It also tracks with where Alphabet has pointed itself. Under Pichai, AI now runs through Search, Cloud and the Gemini family of models a shift the company's own regulatory filings describe as central to its strategy. A prediction about AI spreading into everyday work is, conveniently, also a description of Google's product roadmap.On India, Pichai said the country is increasingly producing innovations that can benefit the whole world, and that an "ambitious, optimistic new generation of Indians" has the chance to reimagine what's possible. AI can amplify that potential, he argued, but universities are what keep it useful to everyone rather than to a narrow few—a point that doubles as the institute's brief for its next 25 years.Much of the current momentum, he said, is coming from students. He recalled meeting Gemini Student Ambassadors from across India at the AI Impact Summit in Delhi this year: "Their enthusiasm for how technology can improve lives was palpable, and it's why I'm so optimistic about the future." The role of IIT Kharagpur, he added, "will only grow in importance as you lead the next wave of technology."The institute responded by calling the message a reflection of "the enduring global impact of the IIT ecosystem," saying it now looks ahead "to nurture ideas, inspire generations and create solutions that make a difference to India and the world."After Kharagpur, Pichai went to Stanford and then Wharton. He joined Google in 2004, worked on Toolbar and Chrome before taking charge of product and engineering across its major platforms, became CEO in 2015, and added Alphabet in December 2019.
Article Summary: Google ceo sundar pichai has recorded a video message for iit kharagpur as the institute turns 75. He uses the anniversary to set out where he thinks artificial intelligence lands over the next five years. He says universities, not just tech companies, will decide whether any of it reaches people who aren't already using it.

Article Title: Amazon to hire 160,000 temporary workers this festive season
Article Text:
Amazon rejects allegations of consumer harm

Ahead of the upcoming festive season, Amazon India has announced that it has created more than 160,000 seasonal work opportunities across its pan India operations network that supports its ecommerce and quick commerce business. These include direct and indirect work opportunities across 400 cities in India, spanning large metros as well as tier 2 and 3 cities like Varanasi, Kochi, Jalandhar, Ghaziabad, Ranchi, Salem, Gorakhpur, and others. The new associates will join Amazon’s existing pan-India operations network helping pick, pack, ship, and deliver customer orders safely and reliably while supporting the growing demand during the festive period. Amazon has already onboarded the majority of these associates in preparation for the festive season and has begun providing them with the necessary training.As part of Amazon’s commitment to supporting its associates, even the seasonal associates will have access to the range of safety and welfare programs and benefits that other associates have. This includes benefits like a safe, supportive and inclusive workplace, safety, financial and social security.Through its Samridhi program, Amazon will also support associates joining the company’s operations network ahead of the festive season to enroll on the e-shram portal and access other government welfare and social security programs.“We are committed to providing customers across every pin-code in India with fast and reliable deliveries this festive season. To meet the anticipated increase in customer demand, we have created over 1.6 lakh seasonal work opportunities across our operations network. As we focus on building one of India’s largest, safest, fastest and most reliable operations network, we are also committed to building an inclusive workforce, with opportunities for thousands of women associates and persons with disabilities. This expanded workforce will help us strengthen our fulfillment and logistics capabilities and ensure we can handle the festive season seamlessly. Many of these associates continue their journey with Amazon beyond the festive period, while several others return year after year to work with us,” said Abhinav Singh, VP, Operations, Amazon India, APAC, Middle East, Africa and Turkiye.Amazon India claims to have fulfilment centers spread across 15 states, offering over 43 million cubic feet of storage space for seller inventory; sortation centers in 19 states; along with a network of close to 2,000 Amazon-operated and partner delivery stations. Also, it has 28,000 'Hub delivery' partners and thousands of Amazon Flex partners, who are ready to deliver smiles to customers across the country.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos: “I knew that if I failed I wouldn’t regret that, but…” - a lesson about risk, failure and regret
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos

“I knew that if I failed I wouldn’t regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not trying.”

What Jeff Bezos meant by the quote

The modest beginnings behind a much bigger company

The long-term view behind a risky choice

Why failure mattered less to him than uncertainty

A lesson about decisions rather than ambition

Trying can be smaller than people think

Lessons to learn from Jeff Bezos’ quote

Failure is not always the worst outcome

Consider the cost of inaction

Think beyond the present moment

Regret can be a useful decision-making tool

Trying does not always mean taking a huge risk

Do not confuse uncertainty with failure

Security has a cost too

A decision does not need a guaranteed outcome to be worthwhile

Learn to separate fear from judgement

The goal is not to avoid every mistake

There are decisions that become difficult precisely because both choices carry a cost. Staying where things are familiar can offer security, while taking a chance can leave a person facing an outcome that cannot be predicted. Jeff Bezos encountered that dilemma in the 1990s, when he was working at the investment firm D. E. Shaw began considering an idea built around the rapidly expanding internet. Leaving a well-paid job for an online bookseller was hardly a guaranteed route to success. Bezos knew the business could fail. What mattered to him was a different possibility: that years later, he might look back and wish he had given the idea a chance. He eventually left his job and founded Amazon . The decision became one of the defining moments of his career, but the reasoning behind it came before anyone knew how the company would turn out.Bezos was describing the way he weighed the risk of leaving his established career. He did not know whether Amazon would succeed. In fact, he considered failure a realistic possibility.His thinking centred on regret rather than prediction. He imagined himself much older and considered how he might view the decision with the benefit of hindsight.If the business failed, he would at least know that he had attempted it. If he stayed in his job and never tried, there would be no answer to the question of what might have happened.The quote is therefore not simply about being unafraid of failure. It is about recognising that inaction can also have consequences. Sometimes the safest decision in the short term can leave a person with a longer-lasting question.It is easy to view the original Amazon through the scale of the company that exists today. That can distort what Bezos was actually deciding in 1994.Amazon did not begin as a plan to create a vast technology and retail company. It began as an online bookstore. The first version of the business was focused on selling books through a website at a time when buying something online was still unfamiliar to most people.The company opened its virtual doors in July 1995.Within its first weeks, Amazon had shipped books across the United States and to customers overseas. The catalogue also gave the business an advantage that physical shops struggled to match. It could offer a huge range of titles without having to keep every book on shelves.The early success did not prove that Bezos had known what would happen. It showed what happened after he decided to try.The phrase most closely associated with Bezos's decision is his “regret minimisation framework”.Rather than trying to predict every detail of the future, he imagined reaching old age and looking back at the choice. From that imagined future perspective, he considered which decision was more likely to cause regret. The framework simplified the problem. If Amazon failed, Bezos could return to the job market and continue with his career. If he never tried, he might spend years wondering whether the business could have worked.It was not a mathematical formula. It was a way of changing the time frame of the decision. A difficult choice in the present can look different when viewed from decades later.Failure produces an answer. If a business closes, a person knows that a particular approach did not work. If an application is rejected, there is a definite outcome. Even an unsuccessful project can reveal what needs to change.Not trying provides none of that. The possibility remains hypothetical. There is no evidence showing whether the idea could have succeeded or failed.For Bezos, that unresolved possibility was harder to accept than failure itself. That is perhaps the most precise way to understand the quote. He was not claiming that failure feels good. He was saying that failure was an outcome he could live with, while never making the attempt might leave a question that could not be settled.The quote can be applied without turning every difficult choice into an entrepreneurial gamble. A person considering a career change, a new qualification, a business idea or a creative project might ask a similar question: which outcome would be harder to live with years from now?Sometimes the responsible decision is to stay put. Financial obligations, family circumstances, timing and the consequences of failure all matter. Bezos's framework cannot account for every situation.What it can do is introduce another consideration into the decision, the cost of never finding out.There is also no need for “trying” to involve quitting a job or risking a life's savings.It might mean testing an idea on a small scale. Applying for an opportunity. Taking a course. Speaking to someone in an industry you are considering. Building a first version of a project before deciding whether to pursue it seriously.Those steps can reduce uncertainty without requiring an immediate leap. In that sense, the useful part of Bezos's thinking is not necessarily the size of the risk he took. It is the way he separated the fear of failure from the question of future regret.
Article Summary: Jeff bezos said he would not regret leaving his job to start amazon. He did not know whether the company would succeed. He considered failure a realistic possibility. He imagined himself much older and how he might view the decision with the benefit of hindsight. There is no evidence showing whether the idea could have succeeded or failed.

Article Title: Apple follows Google Maps, renames Lake Ontario to Lake America; US President calls change of names 'complete, ratified, and binding'
Article Text:
Apple follows Google Maps with Lake America name change

Apple follows Google Maps with Lake America change

Canada continues to call it Lake Ontario

MapQuest refuses to rename the lake

After Google Maps, Apple Maps has now renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the US after a presidential executive order. The update means Apple users in the United States will see ‘Lake America’ when viewing the Great Lake that sits between New York and Canada’s Ontario province. Users outside the US will continue to see the lake as Lake Ontario. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), US President Donald Trump called the name change 'complete, ratified, and binding'.“Apple Maps has just announced that it has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, so now that very important change of names, between Google Maps and Apple Maps, is complete, ratified, and binding. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” Trump wrote in the post.Google Maps changed its display label for Lake Ontario over the weekend, saying it was following the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which had formally changed the name in the United States. Google then said its Maps service would show different names depending on the user’s location. People in the US would see “Lake America”, users in Canada would see “Lake Ontario”, while users outside the US and Canada would see both names.Canadian officials have rejected the name change and said the country will continue using Lake Ontario in its official records. Prime Minister Mark Carney has pointed to the history of the name, saying it is more than 400 years old and comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io.“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney said.Notably, not every mapping service has followed Google and Apple. MapQuest has rejected the request to use “Lake America”. The company posted a screenshot showing the name Lake Ontario with the message: “We’re not changing it.” According to a Guardian report, the move reportedly helped MapQuest rise to the top of Apple’s US App Store rankings.
Article Summary: Apple follows google maps with lake america name change. Users in the us will see ‘lake america’ when viewing the great lake. Users outside the us and canada will continue to see lake ontario. Canadian officials have rejected the name change and said the country will continue using lake ontario in its official records.
